Newly hatched larvae of the inquiline snailfish emerge after approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days] of incubation at a stable water temperature of 8.1 °C [T = 8.1 °C], an interval that aligns with the prolonged developmental rates typical of high-latitude liparids. Upon eclosion, these yolk-sac larvae possess a wet weight of just 0.000065 grams [Wwb = 0.000065 grams], a figure derived from the average egg diameter of 0.5 millimeters and reflecting the modest maternal investment per offspring that characterizes this species. The larvae remain entirely endotrophic during this initial phase, absorbing their yolk reserves before the onset of first exogenous feeding. This remarkably small initial mass, less than a tenth of a milligram, underscores the vulnerability of the early life stages and the necessity of a productive nursery habitat for successful recruitment.

Metamorphosis in the inquiline snailfish occurs when individuals reach a total length of 1.9 centimeters , marking the transition from a pelagic, planktonic larva to a benthic juvenile. This morphological transformation involves the reorganisation of the body plan and the onset of scale formation, accompanied by a shift from the open water column to a demersal existence in close association with seafloor structures. The total length at metamorphosis is notably small compared to that of congeneric species, suggesting that this liparid adopts a relatively abbreviated larval phase. Following settlement, juveniles commence exogenous feeding on small benthic invertebrates. The subsequent growth trajectory is rapid, as immature post-settlement individuals must accumulate sufficient somatic tissue to reach the size threshold required for the onset of gonadal activity.

Sexual maturation in Liparis inquilinus is attained once individuals achieve a total length of 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters], a size at which the wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 0.6 grams [Wwp = 0.6 grams] based on the species-specific length-weight relationship. Puberty marks the commencement of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, activities that demand considerable energetic resources. The relatively modest size at which reproductive maturity is reached, compared to the ultimate total length of 7.1 centimeters [Li = 7.1 centimeters], indicates a life-history pattern in which reproduction commences well before somatic growth has ceased. This strategy is common among small-bodied, iteroparous teleosts inhabiting energetically variable environments, as it allows some reproductive output even when conditions are not optimal for reaching maximum size.

Reproductive output in this species is considerable for its body size; at a temperature of 8.1 °C [T = 8.1 °C], females produce approximately 3.1 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3.1 eggs per spawning event] and can complete roughly 366 spawning events each year [F_R_i = roughly 366 spawning events each year], yielding a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 3.1 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 3.1 eggs per day]. This high-frequency, low-clutch-size reproductive mode is characteristic of a continuous spawner, wherein gamete release occurs almost daily under favourable thermal conditions. The maximum recorded adult body mass in this species is 2.52 grams [Wwi = 2.52 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship parameterised from field-caught specimens. The combination of a short generation time and sustained reproductive effort allows the inquiline snailfish to maintain stable populations despite the modest size of individual clutches.

Longevity records for the inquiline snailfish indicate that individuals can survive for up to 4745 days [am = up to 4745 days] under the prevailing thermal regime of 8.1 °C [T = 8.1 °C]. This remarkably long lifespan, spanning nearly thirteen years, is unusual for a fish species with a maximum total length of only 7.1 centimeters and is more typical of species inhabiting stable, cold-water environments where metabolic rates are suppressed. The protracted lifespan allows for many reproductive seasons, compensating for the relatively modest size-specific fecundity per event. The ultimate wet weight of 2.52 grams is achieved asymptotically over several years, with growth slowing considerably after the onset of sexual maturity. This life-history configuration, featuring a small body size, high reproductive frequency, and extended senescence, positions Liparis inquilinus as an outlier among related Liparis species, most of which exhibit shorter lives and larger terminal sizes.
